summary: Proposes a lightweight reranker on top of a frozen ToolRet-BGE retriever with two small MLP heads (query-tool relevance, tool-level risk), a tunable safety/utility weight λ, ToolGraph score smoothing, and an optional rule filter. It labels 6,108 tools in UltraTool and Seal-Tools with 5-level risk via three LLM annotators, and defines exposure metrics (RVR@5, SRR@5, sNDCG@5). It reports better relevance-safety trade-offs than relevance-only rerankers.

claims.claim: Core+Graph reranker improves relevance over the strongest baseline on UltraTool.
claims.evidence: Table 2: NDCG@5 0.562 vs ToolRet-BGE 0.429; MRR 0.625. Ours scores the full tool pool while the 8 baselines rerank ToolRet-BGE top-100, so the setups differ; under matched top-100 candidates Core+Graph gets 0.621 NDCG@5 (App. E.2). Means over 3 seeds, SDs in App. E.1.

claims.claim: Rule-filtered variant substantially reduces risky-tool exposure.
claims.evidence: Table 2: UltraTool RVR@5 0.073 and SRR@5 0.019 vs ToolRet-BGE 0.176/0.078; Seal-Tools RVR@5 0.007 vs 0.020. The rule filter consumes the same LLM-derived risk labels used for evaluation, so the reduction is partly circular.

claims.claim: Risk labels are reliable enough to supervise and evaluate.
claims.evidence: Human audit of 150 tools: 60.0% exact agreement, quadratically weighted κ=0.362; Krippendorff α 0.523 on UltraTool across LLM annotators. Human auditor rated health/financial access more conservatively.

claims.claim: Retrieval-stage filtering reduces the action space exposed to agents before execution.
claims.evidence: Only a qualitative 6-query inspection (Table 8). No downstream agent execution, task success, or attack-based evaluation.

patterns.note: Risk-aware top-k tool exposure as a way to shrink and safen the tool catalog; evidence is retrieval metrics only.
Rule filter with risk caps and permission constraints over an audited tool registry; no runtime enforcement evaluated.
Embedding retrieval over tool descriptions with learned heads.

methodology.sample: UltraTool: 2,032 tools, 1,000 test queries; Seal-Tools: 4,076 tools, 700 test_in + 654 test_out queries.
methodology.baselines: ToolRet-BGE plus 8 general-purpose rerankers (MiniLM CE, BGE-reranker-v2-m3, mxbai, MonoT5, Qwen2 rerankers). None of them is risk-aware, so the safety comparison is against methods that do not try to reduce risk.
methodology.variance: 3 seeds; means in main tables, SDs in App. E.1.
methodology.ablations: Component analysis (§5.3), λ sweep (§5.4), stress tests (§5.6).

biases.detail: Safety gains are measured against relevance-only rerankers that have no risk objective; no risk-aware or permission-filter baseline (e.g., a simple metadata filter over the same labels).
Risk labels from Claude Code/Codex/Qwen voting are both training supervision and the evaluation ground truth; human agreement κ=0.362 is low.
RVR/SRR measure exposure of risky tools in top-5, not whether an agent misuses them or whether tasks still succeed.
Synthetic tool benchmarks (UltraTool, Seal-Tools), not real MCP catalogs.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, seeds and SDs reported, and code released. But the safety metric is circular with weak LLM-derived labels, the baselines are risk-unaware, and nothing is shown at the level of agent behaviour.
applicability: Mostly indirect. A team running a small, curated MCP tool set (≤15 tools, per the repo invariants) does not need learned tool retrieval at all. The transferable idea is to attach a risk level and permission metadata to each tool and filter exposure deterministically per task (e.g., write/delete tools for content stores hidden during read-only ingestion analysis). That is a policy-as-code rule the CLI can enforce identically across mixed agent hosts, not a learned reranker. Healthcare-adjacent data access is exactly where the human auditor disagreed with LLM labels, so risk labels for tools touching learner or PHI-like data should be set by humans.
